extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, psychometricians, and researchers validating or adapting personality/humor questionnaires (scale developers, humor researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Adaptation and psychometric validation of the State-Trait Cheerfulness Inventory (long 106-item and standard 60-item forms) into English, including item construction, factor structure, reliability, validity, and translation procedures. Intended to guide scale adaptation and evaluation for humor-related temperamental traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-Trait model: three traits/states
rubrics_metrics.description: The State-Trait Model of Cheerfulness defines three relevant states and traits: state and trait cheerfulness, state and trait seriousness, and state and trait bad mood; cheerfulness lowers the threshold for amusement, whereas seriousness and bad mood heighten it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat cheerfulness, seriousness and bad mood as separable yet interrelated higher-order factors (traits and states). Expect negative correlations of cheerfulness with seriousness and bad mood, and positive correlation between seriousness and bad mood. Use this theoretical structure to guide item selection, factor analyses, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item construction criteria for STCI-T <106>
rubrics_metrics.description: Items were chosen to be (1) short and understandable, (2) of diverse content, (3) covering the construct-related behavior and attitudes comprehensively, (4) free of extreme levels of social desirability, (5) suitable for adolescents and adults, (6) not biased toward particular populations, and (7) logically related to the target constructs but not overlapping with similar but irrelevant constructs (Ruch et al., 1996).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating/adapting items ensure brevity, clarity, broad content coverage, low social desirability, cross-age suitability, cultural neutrality, and conceptual specificity. Screen items for overlap with adjacent constructs and for potential cultural/content biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facet-level measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The long trait form (STCI-T <106>) provides scores for three traits and separate analyses of facets: Cheerfulness (5 facets: CH1–CH5), Seriousness (6 facets: SE1–SE6), and Bad Mood (5 facets: BM1–BM5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the long form to measure and analyze facet-level structure when hypothesis/testing requires fine-grained distinctions. Ensure facets are internally consistent and interpretable; report facet reliabilities and correlations to total scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a four-point answering format
rubrics_metrics.description: The questionnaire utilizes a four-point answering format (1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree) for trait and state versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent response format across trait and state instruments. Consider implications for distributional assumptions in factor analyses (ordinal methods may be needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item polarity and negation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the antithetical nature of the three traits, most items were positively poled; negatively-poled items can be prototypical for another trait, so negations were used only when they represented standing expressions used in everyday language (Ruch et al., 1996).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor positive wording to avoid cross-loading due to antonymy; include negatively keyed items sparingly and only when natural language justifies them; carefully check for unintended trait indication from negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report internal consistencies for traits and facets. Ruch et al. reported high trait alphas (e.g., CH α ≈ .89–.93; SE α ≈ .87–.91; BM α ≈ .93–.94) and facet alphas ranging from satisfactory to high (e.g., α = .64 to .91 in original work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for high reliability at the trait level (typically α ≥ .85 for STCI traits) and acceptable reliability for facets (commonly α ≥ .70, noting some facets may be lower). Report alpha, mean corrected item-total correlations, and discuss facets with low alpha.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrected item-to-total correlation (CITC) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use corrected item-to-total correlations to evaluate items; the study considered minimal CITC > 0.30 and reported mean CITCs per facet/scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag items with CITC ≤ 0.30 for revision or removal. Report mean CITC for facets and scales and use CITC as a primary quantitative criterion during item selection and short-form construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item reduction / short-form construction criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Short form selection was guided by (a) the best corrected item-to-total correlation (CITC), (b) consideration of items' content and representation of all facets, (c) roughly equal representation of facets (with core facets given more weight when necessary), and (d) avoidance of very similar items in content or wording (Ruch et al., p.316).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine empirical indices (CITC) with content/facet coverage when building a short form. Ensure the short form preserves construct breadth, avoids redundancy, and prioritizes core facets if equal representation is impossible. Document selection rules and trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial validity: confirmatory factor analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use confirmatory factor analysis to test the postulated underlying structure (three correlated higher-order factors and their facets). The STCI-T <106> and STCI-T <60>/<30> typically show a three-factor structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct CFA (and exploratory analyses where appropriate) to test the theoretical model; report fit indices and compare facet vs. trait-level models. Ensure sample sizes adequate for CFA; consider using appropriate estimators for ordinal data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-trait multi-method (MTMM) approach for convergent/discriminant validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply MTMM and CFA to separate influences due to trait, method, and error components; Carretero-Dios et al. (2011) used MTMM to confirm convergent validity across self-reports, peer-reports and aggregated states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MTMM designs (multiple methods, multiple traits) and CFA to demonstrate convergent validity (homologous scales/methods correlate strongly) and discriminant validity (heterologous correlations lower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test-retest (temporal) stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Report retest stability for traits; prior work found one-month retest correlations between 0.77 and 0.86 for traits (Ruch & Köhler, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess temporal stability of trait measures with appropriate retest intervals; expect high stability for traits and lower stability for states. Include retest correlations and discuss temporal properties vis-à-vis trait/state distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent, discriminant and predictive validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish convergent validity with related humor measures (e.g., SHS, HSQ, CHS, SHRQ) and predictive validity for external criteria (e.g., laughter frequency, pain tolerance, responses to humor interventions). Discriminant validity should show lower correlations to heterologous constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate STCI scales with established humor/personality/well-being measures and with behavioral/experimental outcomes. Demonstrate expected pattern: homologous state–trait correlations high, heterologous lower; report predictive associations with external criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-version sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The STCI-S (state form) was designed to capture mood quality and be sensitive to short-term mood alternations (e.g., experimental manipulations, weather, interventions); facets of state cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood were distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When validating a state measure, test sensitivity to manipulations and naturally occurring mood variations, expect lower test-retest stability than traits, and demonstrate the instrument's ability to detect experimental changes or clinical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid content-saturated items and humor-preference bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrument was constructed to be largely free of content-saturated items and specific humor-material preferences (to improve generalizability across age/cultural groups) — prior criticism of other humor scales motivated this approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer content-general items that index temperament rather than references to specific comedians/jokes/styles. This reduces cultural/age bias and improves cross-population comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-language and population generalizability / measurement invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate translated/adapted versions across languages, nations and respondent types (self, peer, children, workplace) and examine whether the three-factor structure generalizes across samples and languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform cross-language validation and tests of measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar) across countries, age groups, and respondent types. Report any mean differences and discuss cultural or sampling sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation procedure and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The English adaptation used a multi-step translation procedure: independent translations by two experts, comparison and discussion, review by additional experts for orthography/grammar, and discussion with original scale author to form a pilot version. The paper notes a deviation from classical back-translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple expert translators, iterative review, and consultation with original authors; ideally include back-translation and pilot testing. Document each step and justify deviations from classical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample and validation design requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-form validation requires independently collected samples sufficiently large for confirmatory factor analyses; the authors note the STCI-T <60> still needs validation in independent samples with adequate N for CFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan validation studies with adequate sample sizes for CFA and invariance testing. Include independent replication samples, and where possible collect data with both long and short forms and include peer reports to evaluate congruence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-report congruence and multi-informant assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Include peer-report versions and evaluate self- and peer-report congruence; the STCI-T <60> showed good comparability of self- and peer-reports in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multi-informant data (self, peer, parent/teacher for children) to assess convergent validity across raters. Report inter-rater correlations and discuss discrepancies.
